### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, the elapsed time between consecutive completions of A16 and A17 was short: median about 0.06 hours (roughly 4 minutes), mean about 0.09 hours. In the later window it roughly doubled, to a median of about 0.13 hours (8 minutes) and a mean of about 0.17 hours, with the whole distribution shifted upward (quarter point about 0.04 → 0.09 hours, three-quarter point about 0.14 → 0.25 hours) and somewhat more spread. The difference was larger than in about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits. [TWAIT001]
- The elapsed time between consecutive completions of A28 and A17 also roughly doubled: median about 0.78 hours (47 minutes) in the earlier window versus about 1.58 hours (95 minutes) in the later one; mean about 0.79 → 1.60 hours; quarter/three-quarter points about 0.70/0.86 → 1.43/1.77 hours. This difference was also larger than in about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits. [TWAIT002]
- The sequences themselves stayed about equally common: roughly 45 of 200 versus 37 of 200 traces for A16→A17, and 42 versus 41 for A28→A17 (about one in five traces in each window), so the difference lies in the durations, not in how often these sequences occur. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility of a timing change centred on A17: in the later window, the elapsed time between the completion of the preceding activity and the completion of A17 roughly doubled, both after A16 (median about 4 → 8 minutes) and after A28 (about 47 → 95 minutes). Supporting signs: the indicator measures this interval directly, both items show the same direction with all quartiles shifted upward, both differences exceed about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits, and the time family produced 2 qualifying items where only about 0.014 were expected if nothing had changed (control flow: 0 items against about 0.27 expected), so chance is an unlikely explanation for the items as a whole. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Limitations: both items share A17, so they may reflect one underlying change rather than two independent ones; the indicator measures elapsed time between consecutive completions and cannot separate waiting from processing, nor show whether A17 started later, took longer, or the predecessors finished earlier; and a change in intervening completions could in principle stretch the measured gaps, although no control-flow item qualified. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Other differences: none were reported — the only qualifying items in the whole screening were the two timing items above, with no control-flow item qualifying (0 among 55 units against about 0.27 expected by chance). [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Let me analyse this evidence.

Schema: pcr-evidence-2.1. Two windows of 200 traces each.

Screening: 84 units tested, 0.28 items expected without change. By family:
- control_flow: 55 units tested, 0 items, 0.27 expected
- time: 29 units tested, 2 items, 0.014 expected

So the time family has 2 items when only 0.014 would be expected by chance. That's many times larger than the expectation (2 vs 0.014 is ~143x). Per the instructions: "A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole, even when all items describe one underlying difference; do not merge items for this comparison."

So we compare per family: time family has 2 items vs 0.014 expected — that's far above chance expectation. Control flow has 0 items vs 0.27 expected — consistent with no change.

So the count comparison passes: 2 items when fewer than 0.014 expected is not "the same order" — it's many times larger. So we don't automatically go to "Insufficient evidence" via the screening comparison. Then we judge by directness, consistency, and ability to rule out competing explanations.

The two items:
- TWAIT001: T_WAIT between A16 and A17 (elapsed time between consecutive completion events of A16 and A17, presumably). Before: 45 observations, mean 0.089 hours (~5.4 min), median 0.062 h. After: 37 observations, mean 0.166 h (~10 min), median 0.134 h. So the elapsed time roughly doubled. Empirical strength 0.9995 — the difference is larger than in 99.95% of random re-splits. Support: 45 before, 37 after — moderate counts out of 200 traces.

- TWAIT002: T_WAIT between A28 and A17. Before: 42 obs, mean 0.786 h (~47 min), median 0.783 h. After: 41 obs, mean 1.598 h (~96 min), median 1.583 h. Roughly doubled. Empirical strength 0.9995. Support 42/41.

Both items involve A17 as the second activity. Both show a consistent pattern: elapsed time between consecutive completions roughly doubled, with the whole distribution shifted up (q25, median, q75 all increased), and slightly fewer observations.

Interpretation: TWAIT is elapsed time between consecutive completion events. A consistent change in these times is a hypothesis in its own right (a change in timing); it does not need a structural counterpart. So the hypothesis: the time between completion of A16 and A17, and between A28 and A17, increased — i.e., the interval preceding A17's completion lengthened in both sequences. This is a timing change centred on A17 (or on the transitions into A17).

Directness: TWAIT directly measures the timing. Consistency: two items, both involving A17, both showing ~doubling, both with very high empirical strength. Competing explanations: could be sampling variation — but empirical strength 0.9995 each and the screening comparison (2 vs 0.014 expected) makes chance unlikely as a whole. However, with only two items both sharing A17, we can't distinguish whether the change is in A17's completion timing or in the preceding activities. Also, both items involve A17, so they may reflect the same underlying behaviour — not independent confirmations. Also note: TWAIT is elapsed time between consecutive completion events; it could reflect waiting, service, or other delays — we shouldn't call it pure waiting.

Also, control flow shows no items — no structural change detected. So the hypothesis is a pure timing change.

Support level: The screening comparison passes (2 items vs 0.014 expected in the time family). The evidence is direct (TWAIT measures timing directly), consistent (both items show the same direction and magnitude pattern, both centred on A17). Can we rule out competing explanations? The main competing explanation is random sampling variation, which the empirical strength (0.9995 for both) and the family-level screening comparison argue against. Another competing explanation: the two items share A17, so they might be one behaviour rather than two — but that doesn't undermine the timing hypothesis; it actually localises it.

Hmm, is this "Supported hypothesis" or "Weak hypothesis"? The instructions: "Supported hypothesis: the evidence supports a specific hypothesis directly and consistently." Two TWAIT items, both direct measures of the timing, both showing the same change (roughly doubling of the interval into A17), both with empirical strength 0.9995, and the family screening showing 2 items vs 0.014 expected — that's direct and consistent. The count is many times the chance expectation. I'd say "Supported hypothesis" for a timing change: the elapsed time between the completions of A16 and A17, and of A28 and A17, roughly doubled in the later window.

But wait — caution: "Treat proportions based on few observations as weak." Support 45/37 and 42/41 out of 200 traces — that's about 20-23% of traces containing these pairs within... actually TWAIT support is defined? The support definition lists OCC, POS, DIR, REL, LAG but not TWAIT. For TWAIT, count is the number of consecutive completion pairs (45 before, 37 after). These are moderate counts. The distributions are fairly tight (std ~0.07-0.23 h). The shift is large relative to the spread: for TWAIT001, mean shift 0.077 h vs before std 0.069 h — about 1.1 std. For TWAIT002, shift 0.81 h vs before std 0.11 h — about 7 std. Both with empirical strength 0.9995 (max possible given 2000 references is 1 - 1/2001 ≈ 0.9995, so both are at the ceiling).

Given the directness of TWAIT for timing, the consistency of direction, the shared involvement of A17, and the screening comparison, I lean "Supported hypothesis" for a timing change around A17. The limitation: we cannot tell from these items whether the delay arises before A17's completion generally or is specific to the two predecessor activities; also elapsed time between completions may include waiting and processing, so the cause (queueing vs. handling) is not identifiable. Also, both items share A17 so they may reflect one underlying change, not two independent ones.

Actually, let me reconsider whether "Weak hypothesis" is more appropriate. The guidance says a hypothesis about timing is a hypothesis in its own right. The evidence: 2 items in time family vs 0.014 expected — "a count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole". So chance is largely ruled out at the family level. Directness: TWAIT directly measures the timing between these activity pairs. Consistency: both items agree in direction and roughly in relative magnitude (doubling). Competing explanations: the main one would be that the change is not specific to these pairs but a general slowdown — but we only have these two items; other pairs didn't qualify. Hmm, actually a general slowdown affecting all pairs would likely produce more qualifying items (29 time units tested, only 2 qualified). So the change appears localised to transitions into A17. One competing explanation we can't rule out: whether the increase is due to A17 itself being completed later (e.g., A17's own execution taking longer or starting later) versus the predecessors A16/A28 completing earlier relative to A17 — the indicator measures the gap between consecutive completions, so both interpretations fit. Also, elapsed time includes any waiting plus processing; we can't separate them.

I think "Supported hypothesis" is defensible: direct (TWAIT measures exactly the timing), consistent (two pairs, same direction, both involving A17, both at ceiling empirical strength), chance largely excluded by the family screening (2 vs 0.014). The limitation is that the two items share A17 and thus may be one behaviour, and the indicator cannot distinguish waiting from processing time.

I'll go with "Supported hypothesis" for a timing change: the elapsed time from the completions of A16 and of A28 to the completion of A17 roughly doubled in the later window.
